The review states that Lythraceae contributes one reported heterantherous species. Nepi, Guarnieri & Pacini 2003 (Plant Biology 5:311-314; DOI 10.1055/s-2003-40797) independently identifies L. indica as heterantheric with reproductive long stamens and feed-pollen short stamens. This is an independent pre-2010 resolution, not a claim that Supporting Table S1 was accessed.

Independent pre-2010 family representative, not Table S1 transcription. Darwin's herbarium manuscript records M. lepidota as certainly having two stamen lengths in the same flower. Spruce's 1876-77 species list includes M. lepidota among Mollia with five longer outer cohorts bearing green pollen and five shorter inner cohorts bearing yellow pollen. Maguire's 1978 species treatment independently describes five outer stamen phalanges about 2 cm long and five inner phalanges about 1.5 cm long. Current Kew taxonomy places M. lepidota in Malvaceae. This closes the independent representative need without claiming that the inaccessible 2010 Table S1 specifically listed this species.

Independent species-level resolution, not Table S1 transcription. Flora of North America / Hodgson's Bixaceae treatment describes Amoreuxia as having two dimorphic fertile stamen sets; A. wrightii specifically has shorter distal filaments with yellow anthers and longer proximal filaments with usually dark-red anthers. APG-style sources place Amoreuxia in Bixaceae, consistent with the review's merger of Cochlospermaceae into Bixaceae.

The review states that Brassicaceae contributes one reported heterantherous species. Kudo 2003 (Functional Ecology 17:349-355; DOI 10.1046/j.1365-2435.2003.00736.x) independently experiments on long and short B. rapa stamens and demonstrates different pollination contributions. This is an independent pre-2010 resolution, not a claim that Supporting Table S1 was accessed.

Independent pre-2010 family representative, not Table S1 transcription. Manning & Brothers 1986 directly describe marked heteranthery in D. anastrepta: the anticous anther pair is greatly reduced and produces little or no yellow pollen, whereas the posticous pair associated with the stigma produces copious grey-green pollen. Hilliard & Burtt published the species in 1983, and current Kew taxonomy retains D. anastrepta in Scrophulariaceae. This closes independent representative provenance without claiming that the inaccessible 2010 Table S1 listed this species.
